problem: A loss ballad has to fit more than one kind of loss (someone who left, someone who died), and every draft either names the circumstance or goes vague.
technique: Open it through grammar, not vagueness: write to 'you' in the past tense, keep the narrator's needs and admissions plain and concrete, and cut only the facts that would say why the person is gone (no new partner, no funeral). A title that makes the narrator the object of the other person's past love holds both readings.
example: Capaldi says he wanted 'Someone You Loved' to be about losing someone in general, to fit both a relationship ending and family bereavements (NME; SongwriterUniverse). The title is past tense with the narrator as object, and his later accounts of the subject vary without contradicting it. The opposite route: Dan Wilson says he and Adele made 'Someone Like You' as personal as possible, with a married ex and an uninvited visit.
limits: The widening is a documented statement; the grammatical mechanism is the analyst's reading of the title, not checked against a full lyric. Lexical; no audio needed.
when_not: Critics call the open version generic (Stereogum, New Statesman), and it relies on a voice that supplies the particulars. A song whose force is a scene loses its point when opened.
distinct_from: C23: anchors an unnamed addressee with one concrete image; this card opens the addressee through tense and pronoun and deliberately avoids any image that would settle it
C31: a double reading of an everyday time phrase that the verses keep open; here the double reading is of why the person is absent
C12: choose portable plainness or particular specificity; this card is how to build the portable version without going vague

problem: A ballad chorus makes a brave claim (I'm moving on, I'll be fine) and it sounds either untrue or smug.
technique: Keep the brave claim and add one small qualifier that confesses the opposite ('like', 'almost', 'still', 'mostly'). Let the verses state the real wish plainly, so the chorus can be sung with full sincerity and still mean the reverse.
example: Dan Wilson says the 'Someone Like You' chorus is ironic: she says she'll find someone else, but what she wants is someone like him. The verses set up the married ex and her uninvited visit.
limits: The irony reading is the co-writer's documented statement; extending it to other qualifiers is the analyst's. Lexical; no audio needed.
when_not: If the verses don't make the real wish clear, listeners hear only the surface claim. A genuinely defiant song should not undercut itself.
distinct_from: C30: picks the angle that turns a title phrase against its usual sense; this card keeps the usual sense on the surface and lets one qualifier carry the confession
C28: concedes someone else's maxim and admits failing it; here the narrator's own resolve carries its contradiction
C31: keeps two readings open; here the verses settle which one is true

problem: In a sincere ballad written for an artist (or pitched to several), a key line contains a word that genders the addressee or fixes the singer's identity.
technique: Before locking the line, ask whether that word is doing story work. If it is, keep it. If it only fills the slot, try a word that keeps the line true for this singer later and for other voices, and mark it as a deliberate choice.
example: Sam Smith says a gendered word in the second line of 'Stay With Me' became hard to sing after they came out as non-binary. With Jimmy Napes's agreement they changed it live from December 2022, calling the replacement imperfect but the closest feeling; the 2024 re-recording carries the change.
limits: One documented case; the benefit for pitching to several artists is the analyst's extension. Lexical; no audio needed.
when_not: Specific words are often a song's strength (C11), and a friend told Smith to leave the song as a snapshot. Don't neutralise a detail that makes the story.
distinct_from: C02: whether this singer would say the line now; this card asks whether they, or another singer, can still sing it truthfully later
C11: choose one specific, checkable detail; this card separates specifics that carry story from words that only fix identity
